newsitem.title: JAPAN: Prosecutors join nuclear accident investigation.
newsitem.headline: Prosecutors join nuclear accident investigation.

text.p: Police investigating a falsified report on Japan's worst nuclear accident asked prosecutors to look into the affair on Thursday, signalling indictments might be imminent in the case.
The decision to bring prosecutors into the investigation means that a decision has to be made on whether there should be indictments of officials involved.
The March 11 accident at the state-run Power Reactor and Nuclear Fuel Development Corp's (PNC) nuclear fuel reprocessing plant exposed 37 workers to low-level radiation.

The PNC itself and six of its senior employees -- including PNC Vice Director Kenji Koyama -- are suspected of writing a report falsely claiming to have visually checked that a minor fire in the plant had been extinguished.
An explosion at the site nine hours later exposed the 37 workers to radiation.
Thursday's step came a day after PNC President Toshiyuki Kondo was summoned for questioning by police.
The PNC has come under heavy public criticism for a series of accidents at its facilities, as well as for its attempts to cover up or play down the seriousness of the incidents.

Its prototype fast-breeder reactor Monju, on the Sea of Japan coast, remains closed after a 1995 accident in which sodium coolant leaked. No radiation leaked into the environment as a result of the accident.
A PNC official who was questioning colleagues as part of an in-house investigation committed suicide after it was revealed that the nuclear firm had a secret videotape of the accident.

In April this year, the Science and Technology Agency ordered the PNC to halt operations at its Fugen advanced heavy-water reactor after learning that the firm had delayed reporting a radiation leakage. Fugen resumed operation in June.
The PNC is due to be dismantled with some of its business scheduled to be scrapped or shifted to the private sector.
However two key businesses -- the fast-breeder reactor development programme and research and development on radioactive wast management -- will remain under government control.
The two programmes are the pillars of energy-poor Japan's nuclear policy.
